hook_text: For two hundred years, people said development meant factories. What if there were other roads?
clip_script: In 1969 the Makuleke people were forced off their land in the Kruger Park. In 1998 they won it back. They could have ploughed it. Instead they kept it wild, and now tourists pay to stay there, funding schools and bursaries. In Bangladesh, an economist lent a few dollars each to poor women with no property at all. They paid him back, built businesses, and his bank went on to help millions. In Kenya, people who had never had a bank account began sending money by cellphone. In South Africa, workers earn wages by clearing thirsty alien trees and saving water. And neighbours pool their money every month in stokvels. None of these needed a smokestack. Big projects still matter: dams, power stations, highways. But development works best when the people who live with it help to shape it.
visual_style: Elephants crossing a river beside a lodge; a woman's hands receiving a few coins and then selling vegetables; a phone screen showing a money transfer; workers cutting down tall alien trees beside a stream; a stokvel meeting around a table.
pacing: A sequence of short scenes, building to a confident close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to explore alternatives to industrialisation and how communities shape development.
